newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-ALPHAND WINS AS PISTE TAKES ITS TOLL.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-ALPHAND WINS AS PISTE TAKES ITS TOLL.

text.p: Luc Alphand, surprising himself with his determination, won his second Alpine skiing World Cup downhill of the season on Sunday on a treacherous piste that claimed several rivals.

Alphand, winner of the men's World Cup downhill title for the past two seasons, clocked two minutes 0.51 seconds down the steep and icy Stelvio piste bathed alternately in bright sunshine and deep shade through the trees.
"Its a great way to finish the year," said the 31-year-old Frenchman, who has now won eight World Cup races.
William Besse was second in 2:00.72 to become the first Swiss downhiller to step on the podium this season.
Kristian Ghedina, Alphand's main rival after four downhills, was third in 2:01.18 and the first Italian on the podium in Bormio since the resort first hosted a race in 1993.
Ghedina, who like Alphand won in Val Gardena this month, was pleased but felt luck was not on his side.
The Italian, bearded at Val Gardena but clean shaven in Bormio, shared a room with compatriot Peter Runggaldier who came down with a temperature overnight and slept little.
"I was so tired this morning," said Ghedina. "My legs were burning on the lower part of the course."
Runggaldier started but did not have the strength to keep the racing line and skied out on the upper piste.
He was not the only one, with five of the first eight men on the starting list failing to make the finish.
The race organisers put extra water on the higher turns overnight to harden the piste and hold it together and many of the racers found it hard to control their skis.
Overall World Cup leader Hans Knauss, starting first, almost fell at the Carcentina bend when his skis veered away from under his body and retired halfway down the hill.
Canada's Brian Stemmle skied out at the top, Runggaldier went after him, world champion Patrick Ortlieb did not start due to a stomach bug and Switzerland's Bruno Kernen crashed out.
The race was repeatedly stopped after the main skiers had gone down as several later starters came to grief.
"My first goal at the start was to have a clean run and not to crash," said Alphand after an exemplary run.
The Frenchman said he had been struck by how Austrian Josef Strobl had attacked the piste before he went down.
"I thought these young guys are really crazy," Alphand said. But he clearly took notice because he admitted that he had showed more aggression than he had intended to.
"I surprised myself," he said at the finish. "I didn't think I could be so aggressive. When you have as much experience as me it is much harder to ski to the limit than before."

Alphand rated the Bormio race as one of the three top downhills in the world, adding: "When you win here then you know you are in good shape. I now have to be careful to make sure I stay on form for the next five weeks."
The world championships in Sestriere, Italy, start in February and Alphand's main aim this season is a world title.

Besse, who has not won a downhill since 1994 and has had only one podium finish since then, was delighted to be back among the front-runners after a long lean period for both him and the once all-powerful Swiss men's team.
"This race has freed me," he said. "I knew I could do well because I ski better when it is more challenging."
The downhillers now have a rest until January 11 when the next race is staged in Chamonix, France.
